To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

a) the discriminative representation of convolutional features in a transformed space is more effective for indoor scene recognition than the original structured representation, and b) the proposed approach achieves a new state-of-the-art performance on five major scene recognition data sets.

the structure-presering property of the convolution features is not of substantial use for indoor scene recognition, and that the discriminative aspects can be encoded in terms of general object categories that commonly appear in indoor scenes.

(i) the discriminative representation of the mid-level features in the convolutional neural networks outperforms the original convolutional features for indoor scene recognition and that (ii) the discriminative features can be learned in a supervised fashion using a large-scale data set that contains a diverse set of object categories.
In summary, our research is concerned with

three important aspects of the indoor scene categorization problem: (i) the need for a more powerful feature representation that captures the discriminative information of the target data, (ii) the need for an object-centric representation that is more robust to the intra-scene variations and the confusing similarities between different scenes, and (iii) the need for large-scale data that can be used to learn more powerful object detectors.

the following contributions: (1) a large-scale data set that is a collection of 1300 general object categories that can be found in indoor scenes, (2) a novel representation of convolutional activations, and (3) a new state-of-the-art performance on indoor scene recognition.
the design of a novel representation of the convolutional features that is highly discriminative and is able to encode scene information in terms of the objects that are present in the scene.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the proposed method outperforms the previous state-of-art methods by a large margin.
the discriminative representation of the mid-level convolutional feature space is a promising direction to explore for scene recognition, especially in indoor scenes.
the proposed method is the best performing method on all five indoor scene recognition data sets.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the proposed method is the first to surpass the human-level performance on indoor scene recognition.
we propose a discriminative representation for convolutional features, which is shown to be effective for indoor scene recognition.
our approach is able to achieve the best reported results for all data sets and for all categories.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the structure-preserv- ing property of convolutional features can be traded off for discriminative power.
the discriminative representation of convolutional features is more effective than the structure-preserving representation of the convolutional activations.
the mid-level representations of convolutional features, when properly transformed to another space, can be highly effective in solving challenging scene classification problems.
